questions.question: A ball is thrown from $S$ at an angle to the horizontal as shown in the diagram. $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ are different positions along the ball's trajectory. Which row of the table best represents the velocity and acceleration of the ball at $X$, $Y$ and $Z$?
questions.answer: The velocity of the ball is always tangent to its path (up and to the right at $X$, horizontal at $Y$, down and to the right at $Z$; it is not zero at $Y$ because the horizontal component is constant). Ignoring air resistance the only force is gravity, so the acceleration is $9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ vertically downward at every point. This is row A.

questions.question: James Clerk Maxwell made significant contributions to physics. Which of the following did Maxwell NOT contribute to our understanding of physics?
questions.answer: Maxwell's equations unified electricity and magnetism, predicted electromagnetic waves and gave their speed ($c=1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}$). The existence of electromagnetic waves was experimentally validated by Hertz (who produced and detected radio waves with an induction coil), not by Maxwell.
options: Unifying electricity and magnetism through equations
Predicting the existence of electromagnetic waves
Predicting the velocity of electromagnetic waves
Validating the existence of electromagnetic waves

questions.question: An electromagnet is attached to the bottom of a light train which is travelling from left to right, as shown. When a large current is passed through the coils of the electromagnet, the train slows down as a direct result of the law of conservation of energy. In which of the following devices is the law of conservation of energy applied in the same way?
questions.answer: The moving electromagnet induces eddy currents in the rail; by Lenz's law these produce a magnetic field that opposes the relative motion between the magnet and the rail, so the train slows (its kinetic energy is transferred to electrical, then thermal, energy). An induction motor works in the same way: the rotating magnetic field induces currents in the rotor (or axle) whose fields oppose the relative motion between rotor and field, so the rotor is dragged round to reduce that relative motion.

questions.question: In an experiment, alpha particles were fired into a thin sheet of beryllium. Unknown radiation was detected. Which of the results below provides the strongest evidence that the unknown radiation is not gamma radiation?
questions.answer: Gamma radiation and neutrons are both uncharged (so neither is deflected by an electric or magnetic field), both are highly penetrating, and both can knock protons out of paraffin. The photoelectric effect is the distinguishing test: gamma photons have energy well above the work function of a metal and will eject photoelectrons, while neutrons will not.
options: The unknown radiation could not be deflected by an electric field.
The unknown radiation had a very high penetrating power.
The unknown radiation caused protons to be ejected from a block of paraffin.
The unknown radiation could not produce the photoelectric effect.

questions.question: A student swings a $20$ g metal ball on the end of a $1.10$ m length of string around his body at a constant angular velocity of $4\pi\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$. The string makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with the horizontal, as shown. What is the magnitude of the centripetal force acting on the ball?
questions.answer:
The ball moves in a horizontal circle of radius $r=1.10\cos30^\circ=0.953$ m. The centripetal force is the net (horizontal) force:
$$F_c=m\omega^2r=0.020\times(4\pi)^2\times0.953=3.0\ \text{N}.$$
(This is not the tension in the string, which acts along the string.)

questions.question: Geiger and Marsden carried out an experiment to investigate the structure of the atom. Which diagram best represents the model corresponding to the results that they obtained?
questions.answer: Almost all alpha particles passed straight through, but a very small number were deflected through large angles (some almost straight back). This led Rutherford to the nuclear model: a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus surrounded by mostly empty space containing the electrons. Diagram A shows a small central nucleus with a few large-angle deflections; the diagrams with a uniformly filled sphere (the plum-pudding model) or with no deflection do not fit the results.

questions.question: When electromagnetic radiation shines on metals, photoelectrons may be emitted. The maximum kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons is plotted against radiation frequency for four metals as shown in the graph. Electromagnetic radiation of wavelength $167$ nm shines upon an unknown metal and the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons is found to be $4.0\times10^{-19}$ J. Based on this information, what is the unknown metal?
questions.answer:
$$f=\frac c\lambda=\frac{3.00\times10^8}{167\times10^{-9}}=1.80\times10^{15}\ \text{Hz},\qquad K_{max}=\frac{4.0\times10^{-19}}{1.602\times10^{-19}}=2.5\ \text{eV}.$$
On the graph the point $(1.80\times10^{15}\ \text{Hz},\,2.5\ \text{eV})$ lies on the line for Be (the line furthest to the right, i.e. with the highest threshold frequency of the three close lines).

questions.question: A proton, p$^+$, enters an electric field between two parallel charged plates (100 V on the top plate, 0 V on the bottom plate, $20$ cm apart) with an initial horizontal velocity of $u\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. After two microseconds, the proton's velocity is in the direction $45^\circ$ from the horizontal. What is the magnitude of the velocity at two microseconds?
questions.answer:
The field is vertical, so it does not change the horizontal component of velocity, which stays $u$. At $45^\circ$ to the horizontal the vertical component must also equal $u$, so
$$v=\sqrt{u^2+u^2}=\sqrt2\,u\approx1.4u.$$
The field strength and plate voltage are not needed.

questions.question: A radioisotope, $X$, undergoes $\beta^-$ decay. On the grid of number of neutrons against atomic number shown, which choice represents the product of the decay?
questions.answer:
In $\beta^-$ decay a neutron changes into a proton: $n\to p^++e^-+\bar\nu$. The daughter nuclide therefore has the atomic number increased by 1 and the neutron number decreased by 1: one square to the right and one square down on the grid. That is $Q$.

(School error: the marking guide's explanation says the nuclide "loses 1 proton and gains 1 neutron" (which describes $\beta^+$ decay, product $P$), but the school's own answer sheet gives $Q$, which is correct.)

questions.question: The gravitational potential energy of a mass positioned at $X$ in the gravitational field of Earth is $U_X$, and for the same mass positioned at $Y$ is $U_Y$. The diagram is drawn to scale (distances are measured from the centre of Earth). What is the value of $\dfrac{U_X}{U_Y}$?
questions.answer:
From the scale diagram $r_X=2.8$ cm and $r_Y=4.2$ cm. Since $U=-\dfrac{GMm}{r}\propto-\dfrac1r$,
$$\frac{U_X}{U_Y}=\frac{r_Y}{r_X}=\frac{4.2}{2.8}=1.5.$$

questions.question: Three identical parallel wires $W_1$, $W_2$ and $W_3$ are positioned as shown, each carrying a current of the same magnitude in the direction indicated ($W_1$ down, $W_2$ up, $W_3$ down). $W_1$ and $W_2$ are a distance $d$ apart, and $W_2$ and $W_3$ are a distance $2d$ apart, with $W_3$ to the right. If the wire $W_1$ exerts a force on wire $W_2$ of $F$, then what is the magnitude and direction of the total, resultant force on $W_2$?
questions.answer: For parallel wires $\dfrac Fl=\dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi}\dfrac{I_1I_2}{r}$, so with equal currents and lengths, $F\propto\dfrac1r$. $W_1$ and $W_2$ carry opposite currents, so they repel: $W_1$ pushes $W_2$ to the right with force $F$. $W_3$ is twice as far away, so its force on $W_2$ has magnitude $\tfrac12F$; $W_3$ and $W_2$ also carry opposite currents, so $W_3$ pushes $W_2$ to the left. The net force is $F-\tfrac12F=\tfrac12F$ to the right.

questions.question:
The radioactive decay of thorium-232 is $^{232}_{90}\text{Th}\to{}^{228}_{88}\text{Ra}+{}^{4}_{2}\text{He}$. Using the information in the table below, what is the energy released as a result of this decay?

| Nucleus or particle | Mass (u) |
|---|---|
| $^{232}_{90}$Th | 232.038055 |
| $^{228}_{88}$Ra | 228.031070 |
| $^{4}_{2}$He | 4.001506 |

Three identical spaceships are near each other at a given time. An astronaut on ship $A$, sitting on a platform on Earth, observes the lengths of the two other spaceships, ship $B$ and ship $C$, as they pass by Earth at $0.75c$ and $0.94c$, respectively, as shown in the diagram (all three travelling in the same direction). What would the astronauts on the two passing ships observe?
questions.answer:
Length contraction depends on the relative speed between the observer and the object: the faster the relative speed, the shorter the object appears.

Astronaut on $B$: $A$ moves past at $0.75c$, while $C$ moves relative to $B$ at only $\dfrac{0.94c-0.75c}{1-0.94\times0.75}=0.64c$. $A$ is moving faster relative to $B$, so $A$ appears shorter than $C$.

Astronaut on $C$: $A$ moves past at $0.94c$ while $B$ moves relative to $C$ at $0.64c$, so $A$ appears shorter than $B$.

Hence $A$ is shorter in both cases (option D). (The school used the Galilean $0.19c$ for the relative speed, which gives the same conclusion.)
options: Astronaut on ship $B$: length of $A$ > length of $C$; astronaut on ship $C$: length of $A$ > length of $B$
Astronaut on ship $B$: length of $A$ > length of $C$; astronaut on ship $C$: length of $A$ < length of $B$
Astronaut on ship $B$: length of $A$ < length of $C$; astronaut on ship $C$: length of $A$ > length of $B$
Astronaut on ship $B$: length of $A$ < length of $C$; astronaut on ship $C$: length of $A$ < length of $B$

questions.question:
The table contains information related to two moons orbiting Mars.

| Moon | Mass (kg) | Orbital radius (m) | Orbital velocity (km s$^{-1}$) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Deimos | $1.476\times10^{15}$ | $2.35\times10^{7}$ | $1.35$ |
| Phobos | $1.066\times10^{16}$ | $9.38\times10^{6}$ | — |

The orbital velocity of Phobos can be determined by using data selected from this table. What is the orbital velocity of the moon Phobos?
questions.answer:
For orbits about the same body, $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$, so $rv^2=GM$ is constant (the moons' own masses do not matter). Then
$$v_P=v_D\sqrt{\frac{r_D}{r_P}}=1.35\times\sqrt{\frac{2.35\times10^{7}}{9.38\times10^{6}}}=2.14\ \text{km s}^{-1}.$$

questions.question: The emission spectra from a selection of metals (Mg, Al, Cu, Li) and an unknown mixture of metals are shown within the visible waveband in the figure. What metals are in the unknown mixture?
questions.answer: Compare distinctive lines: the mixture has the lines at about 540 nm (Mg) and 720 nm (Al), but not the distinctive lines of Cu (about 553 nm) or Li (about 648 nm). The mixture therefore contains aluminium and magnesium.

questions.question: What is the wavelength, in metres, of a photon emitted from a hydrogen atom when an electron in the $n=2$ level makes a transition to the $n=1$ level?
questions.answer: Rydberg formula: $\dfrac1\lambda=R\left(\dfrac1{n_f^2}-\dfrac1{n_i^2}\right)=1.097\times10^7\left(\dfrac1{1^2}-\dfrac1{2^2}\right)=8.23\times10^6\ \text{m}^{-1}$, so $\lambda=1.22\times10^{-7}$ m.

questions.question: Which of the following ideal transformers could be used to convert an input voltage of $40$ volts AC to an output voltage of $8$ volts AC? The number of turns on the two coils of each transformer is shown in the diagram (either coil may be used as the input).
questions.answer: $\dfrac{V_p}{V_s}=\dfrac{N_p}{N_s}$, so $\dfrac{N_p}{N_s}=\dfrac{40}{8}=5$. The only transformer with a turns ratio of $5$ is C: the input is connected to the $30$-turn coil and the output taken from the $6$-turn coil (a step-down transformer). The others have ratios of $1.25$ (or $0.8$), $4.2$ (or $0.24$) and $10$ (or $0.1$).

questions.question: Three polarisers, $P_1$, $P_2$ and $P_3$, were placed in between a light source and a light detector with their polarising axes aligned parallel, as shown in the first diagram. The light detector recorded a light intensity of $I$. Polariser $P_2$ and $P_3$ were then rotated clockwise, $30^\circ$ and $90^\circ$, respectively (second diagram). What light intensity did the light detector record?
questions.answer: Malus' law $I=I_{max}\cos^2\theta$ at each polariser. $P_1\to P_2$: the angle is $30^\circ$, so $I_2=I\cos^2 30^\circ=0.75I$. $P_2\to P_3$: $P_3$ is at $90^\circ$ and $P_2$ at $30^\circ$, so the angle between them is $60^\circ$: $I_3=0.75I\cos^260^\circ=0.1875I\approx0.19I$.

questions.question: The diagram shows some parts of a simple AC motor (a coil $WXYZ$ between the poles of a magnet). Which row of the table correctly describes the direction of the force acting on side $WX$ and the direction of the torque this produces on the coil?
questions.answer: With an alternating current the current in side $WX$ reverses every half cycle, so by $F=BIl$ the force on it reverses direction every $180^\circ$. As the coil also turns through $180^\circ$ in that time, the side that is passing the other pole now carries the reversed current, so the force on the sides always acts so as to turn the coil in the same sense: a motor needs torque in a continuous direction to keep turning, so the torque on the coil remains in a constant direction.
options: Force on $WX$: remains constant; torque on coil: remains constant
Force on $WX$: remains constant; torque on coil: reverses every $180^\circ$
Force on $WX$: reverses every $180^\circ$; torque on coil: remains constant
Force on $WX$: reverses every $180^\circ$; torque on coil: reverses every $180^\circ$

questions.question: In 1981, a German research team produced 5 atoms of the isotope bohrium-262 via the following nuclear reaction: $^{209}_{83}\text{Bi}+{}^{54}_{24}\text{Cr}\to{}^{262}_{107}\text{Bh}+{}^{1}_{0}\text{n}$. Based on the graph of average binding energy per nucleon against mass number, which of the following choices best describes the nuclear process and energetics of this reaction?
questions.answer: Two nuclei combine into a larger nucleus, so the process is fusion (the emitted neutron is not counted as a second nucleus). The reactants ($A\approx209$ and $54$) and the product ($A=262$) lie on the right-hand, falling side of the binding energy curve, and the product ($A=262$) has a lower binding energy per nucleon than $^{209}$Bi, so the product is less stable than the reactants. Energy must therefore be put in for the reaction to proceed: it is endothermic (energy absorbed).

questions.question:
The light from an incandescent bulb passes through a transparent container of cold hydrogen gas before passing through a collimating slit, as shown in the diagram. The collimated light is incident on a digital spectrometer that measures the spectral intensity curve, which is shown on the graph (a smooth black-body curve with peak near $0.85\ \mu$m and small absorption dips at about $0.41$, $0.43$, $0.49$ and $0.66\ \mu$m).

Explain the absorption dips in the curve in terms of the Bohr model of the atom, with reference to the law of conservation of energy.
questions.answer:
The dips are caused by electrons in the cold hydrogen gas absorbing photons. In the Bohr model, electrons in the $n=2$ level (the Balmer series) absorb a photon of exactly the right energy to move to a higher orbit ($n=3,4,5,6$), which has higher energy. By conservation of energy the photon energy must equal the energy difference between the two levels:
$$E_{photon}+E_{i}=E_{f}\ \Rightarrow\ hf=E_f-E_i.$$
Only photons with these specific wavelengths are absorbed (and re-emitted in random directions), so the intensity of light reaching the spectrometer is reduced at these wavelengths, producing narrow dips in the continuous spectrum.

questions.question:
The light from an incandescent bulb passes through a transparent container of cold hydrogen gas before passing through a collimating slit, as shown in the diagram. The collimated light is incident on a digital spectrometer that measures the spectral intensity curve, which is shown on the graph (a smooth black-body curve with peak near $0.85\ \mu$m and small absorption dips at about $0.41$, $0.43$, $0.49$ and $0.66\ \mu$m).

Calculate the temperature of the incandescent globe.
questions.answer:
From Wien's displacement law, $\lambda_{max}=\dfrac bT$. The peak of the curve is at $\lambda_{max}=0.85\times10^{-6}$ m, so
$$T=\frac{b}{\lambda_{max}}=\frac{2.898\times10^{-3}}{0.85\times10^{-6}}=3.4\times10^{3}\ \text{K}\ (3409\ \text{K}).$$

questions.question:
The light from an incandescent bulb passes through a transparent container of cold hydrogen gas before passing through a collimating slit, as shown in the diagram. The collimated light is incident on a digital spectrometer that measures the spectral intensity curve, which is shown on the graph (a smooth black-body curve with peak near $0.85\ \mu$m and small absorption dips at about $0.41$, $0.43$, $0.49$ and $0.66\ \mu$m).

On the same graph, sketch the curve expected if the experiment is repeated with another incandescent globe radiating at a higher temperature. Assume the absorption dips are approximately the same height. Describe your sketch in words.

Thomas Young described an experiment where light was passed through two slits and the subsequent result was projected on to a screen. The diagram shows the results predicted by two different models: Prediction X (two bright bands on the screen, in line with the slits) and Prediction Y (a pattern of many alternating bright and dark fringes). Identify an assumption of EACH model that determines the results on the screen.
questions.answer: Prediction X (two bands, one behind each slit) corresponds to the assumption that light is a stream of particles (corpuscles) travelling in straight lines, so only the paths through the slits are lit. Prediction Y (a series of bright and dark fringes) corresponds to the assumption that light is a wave, so the light diffracts at each slit and the two waves interfere.

questions.question: Thomas Young described an experiment where light was passed through two slits and the subsequent result was projected on to a screen. The diagram shows the results predicted by two different models: Prediction X (two bright bands in line with the slits) and Prediction Y (alternating bright and dark interference fringes). How did Young's results help lead to the reconceptualisation of the model of light?
questions.answer: At the time, Newton's corpuscular (particle) model was the accepted model of light, which predicts two bright bands (Prediction X). Young passed light through two closely spaced narrow slits and observed an interference pattern of alternating bright and dark fringes on the screen (like Prediction Y). Interference (constructive and destructive superposition) is a wave phenomenon that particles in the corpuscular model cannot explain. Young's results therefore supported Huygens' wave model of light and challenged Newton's particle model, so the model of light was reconceptualised from particles to waves.

questions.question: Use the work of TWO scientists to explain how the combination of their experiments led to a better understanding of the electron.
questions.answer:
**J. J. Thomson** passed cathode rays through perpendicular electric and magnetic fields and adjusted them until the deflections cancelled, so that he could measure the charge-to-mass ratio $q/m$ of the particles. He found that it was the same whatever the cathode metal, showing that cathode rays are negatively charged particles (electrons) common to all matter, much lighter than atoms.

**G. P. Thomson** fired a beam of electrons at a thin metal foil (aluminium or gold) with a photographic plate behind it. He observed concentric diffraction rings like those produced by X-rays, which can only be produced by waves, and the spacings agreed with the crystal dimensions. This confirmed de Broglie's hypothesis that electrons behave like waves.

Together, J. J. Thomson's experiment showed that the electron is a particle with a definite charge-to-mass ratio, and G. P. Thomson's showed that it also has wave properties, giving a more complete (wave–particle duality) understanding of the electron.

questions.question:
Two solenoids are mounted on trays as shown. Each tray is suspended by identical strings of negligible mass to a fixed platform, such that each tray can swing freely. Each solenoid is connected to a galvanometer ($G_1$ and $G_2$), and the solenoid on tray 1 is also connected to an open switch and a battery. The total mass of tray 1 is twice that of tray 2. The solenoids are side by side with their axes aligned.

Explain what would be observed when the switch on tray 1 is closed. In your answer, refer to the current in each galvanometer and the movement of the trays until they reach their maximum displacement.
questions.answer:
**Tray 1.** When the switch is closed a steady current flows through solenoid 1 and $G_1$, so $G_1$ shows a continuous reading. Solenoid 1 becomes an electromagnet with a steady magnetic field, with its north pole at the end facing tray 2 (the right-hand end).

**Tray 2.** While the current in solenoid 1 rises from zero to its steady value, the magnetic flux through solenoid 2 (directed towards the right) increases. By Faraday's law, $\varepsilon=-N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$, an emf is induced in solenoid 2. By Lenz's law the induced current opposes the change in flux, so it produces a field directed to the left through solenoid 2: a north pole at its left-hand end (facing solenoid 1). This current flows through $G_2$ in the corresponding direction. Once the current in solenoid 1 is steady the flux no longer changes, so the emf and current fall to zero: $G_2$ gives only a brief flick.

**Motion.** For that brief time the facing ends of the two solenoids are both north poles, so they repel. The forces on the two trays are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction (Newton's third law), so the trays are pushed apart and swing away from each other. The force acts for the same time on each, so the impulse and momentum gained are equal and opposite: $m_1v_1=m_2v_2$ (total momentum stays zero), giving $\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}=\dfrac{m_2}{m_1}=\dfrac12$. Tray 2 (half the mass) therefore leaves with twice the speed of tray 1. Converting kinetic energy to gravitational potential energy ($\tfrac12v^2=gh$), the height gained is proportional to $v^2$, so tray 2 swings out further and rises to about four times the height of tray 1 before both trays momentarily stop (maximum displacement) and swing back.

questions.question:
A scientist was studying the radioactive decay of beryllium-11. His results are shown in the table below.

| Time (s) | Mass of beryllium-11 (g) | $\ln(N_t/N_0)$ |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 32.6 | 0 |
| 7 | 21.8 | $-0.25$ |
| 13 | 16.1 | $-0.55$ |
| 20 | 11.4 | $-0.90$ |
| 24 | 9.3 | $-1.10$ |

Plot the results for time and $\ln(N_t/N_0)$ on a graph (time on the horizontal axis), including a suitable heading, labelled axes and a line of best fit. Describe the graph you would draw.
questions.answer:
A full-mark graph has: an appropriate descriptive heading (e.g. "Radioactive decay of beryllium-11: $\ln(N_t/N_0)$ against time"); time (s) on the $x$-axis and $\ln(N_t/N_0)$ on the $y$-axis, each labelled with units where relevant; a suitable scale so the points fill most of the grid (e.g. $x$ from 0 to 26 s and $y$ from $-1.2$ to $0$); the five points plotted accurately; and a straight line of best fit (drawn with a ruler) with a negative gradient passing close to all the points, as shown.

(Note: the $\ln(N_t/N_0)$ column is the data to plot. The masses in the middle column do not give exactly these values if $N_0$ is taken as the mass at $t=2$ s, so use the logarithm column as given.)

questions.question:
A scientist was studying the radioactive decay of beryllium-11. His results are shown in the table below.

| Time (s) | Mass of beryllium-11 (g) | $\ln(N_t/N_0)$ |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 32.6 | 0 |
| 7 | 21.8 | $-0.25$ |
| 13 | 16.1 | $-0.55$ |
| 20 | 11.4 | $-0.90$ |
| 24 | 9.3 | $-1.10$ |

Use a graph of $\ln(N_t/N_0)$ against time to determine the decay constant of beryllium-11.
questions.answer:
From $N_t=N_0e^{-\lambda t}$, $\ln\dfrac{N_t}{N_0}=-\lambda t$, so the gradient of the graph is $-\lambda$. Using two points on the line of best fit, e.g. $(4,-0.10)$ and $(22,-1.00)$:
$$\text{gradient}=\frac{-1.00-(-0.10)}{22-4}=-0.050\ \text{s}^{-1}\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda=0.050\ \text{s}^{-1}.$$
(Equivalently, using the data points $(2,0)$ and $(24,-1.10)$: $\lambda=1.10/22=0.050\ \text{s}^{-1}$.)

questions.question: Outline a practical investigation to observe the emission spectra of gas discharge tubes.
questions.answer:
1. Clamp a gas discharge tube vertically in a retort stand.
2. Connect the output terminals of an induction coil to the electrodes of the gas discharge tube, and connect the input of the induction coil to a low-voltage DC power supply (through a switch or tapping key). The induction coil provides the high voltage needed to ionise the gas.
3. Turn off the room lights, switch on the power supply so the gas glows, and observe the light through a hand-held spectroscope (or diffraction grating).
4. Record (draw or photograph) the coloured emission lines seen, then repeat with other gases and compare the line patterns.

questions.question: Identify ONE potential hazard associated with performing gas discharge tube investigations, and outline ONE safe work practice which addresses this hazard.
questions.answer:
Hazard: the induction coil produces a very high voltage (risk of electric shock/electrocution). Safe work practice: only touch the circuit when the power supply is switched off (or use a tapping key so the circuit is on only briefly), and do not touch the electrodes or metal terminals while the apparatus is operating.

(Alternative: sparking can produce X-rays, so keep exposure short and keep a distance from the tube; or the tube becomes hot, so allow it to cool before handling.)

questions.question: Using de Broglie's hypothesis, calculate the wavelength of the electron in the first stationary state of the hydrogen atom if its speed is $2.188\times10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.
questions.answer:
$$\lambda=\frac hp=\frac h{mv}=\frac{6.626\times10^{-34}}{9.109\times10^{-31}\times2.188\times10^{6}}=3.325\times10^{-10}\ \text{m}\ (0.3325\ \text{nm}).$$
(The speed is only $0.0073c$, so relativistic effects are negligible.)

questions.question: Describe how de Broglie's hypothesis extended the work of Bohr in explaining the stability of electron orbits in the hydrogen atom.
questions.answer: Bohr proposed that electrons orbit the nucleus only in certain quantised "stationary states" in which they do not radiate energy, but he gave no reason why only those orbits were stable. De Broglie hypothesised that moving particles such as electrons have an associated matter wave, $\lambda=h/mv$. An electron in orbit must then form a standing wave around the orbit, which requires the circumference to be a whole number of wavelengths, $2\pi r_n=n\lambda_n$. Orbits that do not satisfy this would interfere destructively with themselves, so only the standing-wave orbits exist: this gives Bohr's quantised stationary states (and the condition $mvr=nh/2\pi$) and explains why the electron does not radiate unless it moves between these states.

questions.question:
Bubble chambers are used in conjunction with particle accelerators to photographically record the tracks of fast-moving charged particles. An intense magnetic field is applied at right angles to the path of the particles to deflect them according to their charge and momentum. The diagram shows a beam of protons travelling horizontally and entering a liquid hydrogen bubble chamber in a vertical magnetic field of $25.0$ mT. Examination of the photograph taken by the camera, as sketched, shows that the protons were deflected along a circular path of radius $0.280$ m.

Derive an expression for the velocity of a proton from the forces it experiences in this experiment.
questions.answer:
The magnetic force provides the centripetal force:
$$F_B=F_c\ \Rightarrow\ qvB=\frac{mv^2}{r}\ \Rightarrow\ v=\frac{qBr}{m}.$$

questions.question:
Bubble chambers are used in conjunction with particle accelerators to photographically record the tracks of fast-moving charged particles. An intense magnetic field is applied at right angles to the path of the particles to deflect them according to their charge and momentum. The diagram shows a beam of protons travelling horizontally and entering a liquid hydrogen bubble chamber in a vertical magnetic field of $25.0$ mT. Examination of the photograph taken by the camera, as sketched, shows that the protons were deflected along a circular path of radius $0.280$ m.

Calculate the velocity of a proton in the bubble chamber.

Bubble chambers are used in conjunction with particle accelerators to photographically record the tracks of fast-moving charged particles. An intense magnetic field is applied at right angles to the path of the particles to deflect them according to their charge and momentum. The diagram shows a beam of protons travelling horizontally and entering a liquid hydrogen bubble chamber in a vertical magnetic field of $25.0$ mT. Examination of the photograph taken by the camera, as sketched, shows that the protons were deflected along a circular path of radius $0.280$ m.

Outline TWO limitations of applying special relativity to the analysis of the motion of the protons in this experiment.
questions.answer:
1. The speed is too low for relativistic effects to matter. $v=6.70\times10^5\ \text{m s}^{-1}=0.0022c$, so the Lorentz factor is $\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}=1.0000025$, effectively 1; the classical result is accurate and relativity makes no measurable difference.
2. Special relativity applies only to inertial (non-accelerating) frames of reference. The protons move in a circle, so they are constantly accelerating (centripetal acceleration), and the frame of a proton is not an inertial frame.

(School note: the solution writes $6.70\times10^6$ m s$^{-1}$ in this part, a typo for $6.70\times10^5$ m s$^{-1}$; $0.0022c$ corresponds to $6.7\times10^5$.)

questions.question: The graph shows the vertical displacement of a projectile throughout its trajectory on Earth (the maximum height is $17.6$ m and the horizontal range is $60.0$ m, landing at the same height it was launched from). Calculate the initial velocity of the projectile (magnitude and direction).
questions.answer:
**Vertical:** at the maximum height $v_y=0$ at $s_y=17.6$ m. Using $v_y^2=u_y^2+2a_ys_y$ with $a_y=-9.8$:
$$u_y=\sqrt{2\times9.8\times17.6}=18.6\ \text{m s}^{-1}.$$
**Time of flight:** by symmetry, $t=\dfrac{2u_y}{g}=\dfrac{2\times18.57}{9.8}=3.79$ s.

**Horizontal:** $u_x=\dfrac{s_x}{t}=\dfrac{60.0}{3.79}=15.8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

**Initial velocity:**
$$u=\sqrt{u_x^2+u_y^2}=\sqrt{15.83^2+18.57^2}=24\ \text{m s}^{-1},\qquad\theta=\tan^{-1}\frac{18.57}{15.83}=50^\circ\ \text{above the horizontal}.$$

questions.question: A Molniya orbit is an inclined, highly elliptical orbit with a period of 12 hours, designed to provide communications and remote sensing coverage over high latitudes. The diagram shows the orbit, with $P$ the satellite's position at its greatest distance from Earth. Account for the changes in velocity of the satellite as it completes one orbit from position $P$.
questions.answer:
The total energy of the satellite, $E=U+K$ with $U=-\dfrac{GMm}{r}$, is constant. As the satellite falls from $P$ towards Earth its gravitational potential energy decreases (becomes more negative), so by conservation of energy its kinetic energy and speed increase, reaching the maximum at the closest point (perigee). As it moves back out towards $P$, kinetic energy is converted back into potential energy and the speed decreases to its minimum at $P$.

In addition, the gravitational force is not parallel to the satellite's velocity (except at $P$ and perigee), so it continually changes the direction of the satellite's velocity. Since both the speed and the direction change throughout the orbit, the velocity (a vector) is continuously changing.

questions.question: The g-lite was designed to provide light to remote locations that do not have access to electricity. It uses a lowering mass to drive a generator (through a pulley) to illuminate a light globe. Explain the factors that affect the maximum brightness of the light globe. Use mathematical models to support your answer.
questions.answer:
The brightness depends on the electrical power delivered to the globe, which depends on the emf induced in the generator and the resistance of the circuit. There are two parts: the turning system and the generator.

**Turning system (rate at which the generator is turned)**

- *Mass:* a larger mass gives a larger weight, $F_g=mg$, so a larger torque on the pulley and a faster rotation of the generator, and so a higher emf and brightness.
- *Pulley radius:* the torque is $\tau=rF=rmg$, so a larger radius gives more torque on the generator; but a larger radius also has a larger circumference ($C=2\pi r$), so the mass must fall further per rotation (and the lamp runs for a shorter time).
- *Friction* in the pulley or axle reduces the rotation rate and so reduces the brightness.

**Generator**

The induced emf is $\varepsilon=-N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}=-N\dfrac{\Delta(BA\cos\theta)}{\Delta t}$, so the emf increases with:

- stronger magnets (larger $B$);
- a larger coil area $A$;
- more turns $N$ on the coil;
- faster rotation (a shorter time $\Delta t$ for each change of flux).

**Circuit resistance:** thicker coil wire and thicker connecting wires have a lower resistance, so by $V=IR$ (and $P=VI=I^2R$) a larger current flows for the same emf and the globe is brighter.

A larger emf and current therefore give a greater power to the globe and so a greater maximum brightness.

questions.question:
A charged particle, $q_1$, is accelerated from rest between oppositely charged plates $X$ and $Y$ (a distance $d$ apart), before entering a uniform magnetic field (into the page) occupying a square region of side $d$, as shown in the first diagram. The particle strikes plate $Y$ at point $P$, a vertical distance $s$ from its entry point into the magnetic field. Ignore the effect of gravity.

The experiment is repeated with an apparatus that is twice the size (plates $2d$ apart and a field region of side $2d$), as shown in the second diagram. The voltage between the plates and the magnetic flux are the same. An identical particle, $q_2$, is accelerated from rest between the oppositely charged plates, before entering the uniform magnetic field.

Compare the work done on $q_1$ and $q_2$. Justify your answer.
questions.answer:
The work done on $q_1$ and $q_2$ is the same.

*Electric field:* the work done is $W=qV$. The particles are identical (same $q$) and the potential difference $V$ is the same, so the work done by the electric field is the same for both.

*Magnetic field:* the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity (the particle moves in a circular path), so $W=F_\parallel s=0$ for both particles: no work is done by the magnetic field.

So the total work done is the same.

questions.question:
A charged particle, $q_1$, is accelerated from rest between oppositely charged plates $X$ and $Y$ (a distance $d$ apart), before entering a uniform magnetic field (into the page) occupying a square region of side $d$, as shown in the first diagram. The particle strikes plate $Y$ at point $P$, a vertical distance $s$ from its entry point into the magnetic field. Ignore the effect of gravity.

The experiment is repeated with an apparatus that is twice the size (plates $2d$ apart and a field region of side $2d$), as shown in the second diagram. The voltage between the plates and the magnetic flux are the same. An identical particle, $q_2$, is accelerated from rest between the oppositely charged plates, before entering the uniform magnetic field.

Compare the vertical distances travelled by $q_1$ and $q_2$ in the magnetic field.
questions.answer:
From (a) the work done by the electric field is the same, so the particles enter the magnetic field with the same speed: $qV=\tfrac12mv^2\Rightarrow v=\sqrt{2qV/m}$.

In the magnetic field $qvB=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, so $r=\dfrac{mv}{qB}$, i.e. $r\propto\dfrac1B$ for identical particles with the same speed.

The same magnetic flux $\Phi=BA$ is spread over an area $A$ that is four times as large ($(2d)^2$ instead of $d^2$), so $B=\Phi/A$ and $B_2=\tfrac14B_1$. Therefore $r_2=4r_1$.

The particle completes a semicircle and strikes plate $Y$ a vertical distance $s=2r$ from its entry point, so $s_2=4s_1$: $q_2$ travels four times the vertical distance of $q_1$.

questions.question:
A $500$ g metal rod is allowed to slide along a pair of parallel metal rails, $30$ cm apart and tilted at $60^\circ$ to the horizontal. The rails are connected to a DC power supply and switch, which results in a current of $2.8$ A passing through the rod. The apparatus is in a uniform magnetic field of $2.5$ T which is horizontal, directed out of the strong magnet (perpendicular to the plane containing the rails' horizontal direction and the rod), as shown.

What is the force, including its direction, acting on the rod solely due to the magnetic field?
questions.answer:
The rod is horizontal and perpendicular to the field, so
$$F=BIl\sin\theta=2.5\times2.8\times0.30\times\sin90^\circ=2.1\ \text{N}.$$
By the right-hand rule the force is perpendicular to both the rod and the field: it acts vertically upward (not up the rails).

questions.question:
A $500$ g metal rod is allowed to slide along a pair of parallel metal rails, $30$ cm apart and tilted at $60^\circ$ to the horizontal. The rails are connected to a DC power supply and switch, which results in a current of $2.8$ A passing through the rod. The apparatus is in a uniform magnetic field of $2.5$ T which is horizontal, directed out of the strong magnet (perpendicular to the plane containing the rails' horizontal direction and the rod), as shown.

Calculate the initial acceleration of the rod along the rails.
questions.answer:
Weight: $F_g=mg=0.500\times9.8=4.9$ N downward. The magnetic force is $2.1$ N upward, so the net vertical force is $4.9-2.1=2.8$ N downward.

The rod can only accelerate along the rails (inclined at $60^\circ$ to the horizontal), so the component of this vertical force along the rails is
$$F_{net}=2.8\sin60^\circ=2.4\ \text{N}.$$
$$a=\frac{F_{net}}{m}=\frac{2.42}{0.500}=4.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}\ \text{down the rails}.$$

questions.question:
A $500$ g metal rod is allowed to slide along a pair of parallel metal rails, $30$ cm apart and tilted at $60^\circ$ to the horizontal. The rails are connected to a DC power supply and switch, which results in a current of $2.8$ A passing through the rod. The apparatus is in a uniform magnetic field of $2.5$ T which is horizontal, directed out of the strong magnet (perpendicular to the plane containing the rails' horizontal direction and the rod), as shown.

The experiment is repeated with the switch open. Explain why the acceleration of the rod is different with the switch open.
questions.answer:
With the switch open no current flows through the rod, so the magnetic force on it is zero. The only force along the rails is then the component of the weight:
$$a=\frac{mg\sin60^\circ}{m}=9.8\sin60^\circ=8.5\ \text{m s}^{-2}\ \text{down the rails}.$$
This is greater than the $4.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ with the switch closed, because with the switch closed the upward magnetic force opposes part of the weight and reduces the net force down the rails.

questions.question: A spaceship travels to a distant star at a constant speed, $v$. When it arrives, $17.6$ years have passed on Earth but $9.2$ years have passed for an astronaut on the spaceship. What is the distance to the star, as measured by an observer on Earth?
questions.answer:
The astronaut's time is the proper time, $t_0=9.2$ y, and the Earth time is $t_v=17.6$ y: $t_v=\dfrac{t_0}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}$, so
$$\frac vc=\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{t_0}{t_v}\right)^2}=\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{9.2}{17.6}\right)^2}=0.8524.$$
In Earth's frame the trip takes $17.6$ y, so the distance is
$$s=vt=0.8524c\times17.6\ \text{y}=15.0\ \text{light-years}.$$
